article.title: Every ring you don't answer is a job handing itself to the next listing: a missed call text back setup
article.body_markdown:
A customer calling your business is already decided - they chose you off the card, the reviews, the map. The call is the last step, and it is the most fragile one: a big share of calls to small businesses ring out at any given moment, and most callers who hit a ringtone and nothing else do not leave a voicemail. They dial the next listing. A missed call is not a lost moment - it is a customer with their phone still in their hand, and a text that lands inside a minute can catch them before the next thumb-flick.

The setup in this note takes one afternoon:

- **Name the leak first** - calls ring out for five reasons (all hands busy, after hours, closures, the handset nobody hears, spam training), and each needs its own answer, not one heroic fix.
- **The 60-second window** - speed is the whole trick; a plain text in 40 seconds beats a beautiful one at 5 pm, and the automation has to be automatic, not a to-do list nobody does.
- **The one-time setup, five steps** - the SMS rail you already pay for (most VoIP providers have the toggle built in), the ring-all rule, the four templates, the stop rule, and a named owner for every thread.
- **The four messages** - closed, busy, after hours, and the default; business name in every message, one text per missed call, never a drip campaign.
- **Compliance and manners** - the STOP line, staying in the safe transactional case, and the message that matches the hours on the Google card (the "Google said you were open" one-star usually starts as a mismatch).
- **The thread once it starts** - the automation opens the door, a named human finishes it the same day; and the urgent cases ("pipe leaking now") get a ring, not a text.
- **The four traps** - the stale auto-reply ("closed for Christmas" in March), the number nobody monitors, the text that answers nothing, and the rail that texts people *you* called.
- **The four-minute weekly audit** - misses by cause, texts actually sent, same-day human replies, templates still true.

The worked example: a two-chair barbershop whose books had an invisible soft spot - nobody could call between 12 and 1, when both chairs were full. The provider's call log showed a dozen missed calls a week, clustered in exactly that hour. The missed-call toggle, two templates, and ring-all took one Sunday; in month one, missed calls halved and roughly one in three of the rest was recovered by the text - a quiet, recurring leak that had been worth hundreds a month.
